stem: A point robot starts at (0,0) m with goal (12,0) m. The sole polygonal obstacle has vertices (2,−2), (6,−2), (6,1), (10,1), (10,4), (2,4), joined in that order. Both algorithms first hit H=(2,0), then follow the boundary toward (2,−2), continuing in the listed order. Compare Bug1 and Bug2 from that hit until their first boundary departure: where do they leave, and how much boundary distance has each travelled?

options.text: Bug1 leaves at (10,1) after 41 m of boundary travel; Bug2 leaves at (6,0) after 36 m.
Bug1 leaves at (6,0) after 36 m of boundary travel; Bug2 leaves at (6,0) after 8 m.
Bug1 leaves at (10,1) after 13 m of boundary travel; Bug2 leaves at (6,0) after 8 m.
Bug1 leaves at (10,1) after 41 m of boundary travel; Bug2 leaves at (6,0) after 8 m.

assumptions: All coordinates are supplied in metres, not measurements of the source figure. The closed polygon interior is forbidden; ideal boundary following is permitted for a point robot.
The environment is static and otherwise empty. Exact localization and boundary sensing are assumed. Straight outgoing motion at the eligible leave points is locally free.

Bug1 completes one full survey, chooses the globally closest boundary point to the goal, and may reverse direction to use the shorter boundary return. Bug2 retains the original y=0 goal line and the specified boundary-following direction.
Count only distance along this obstacle from the first hit until departure, excluding the start-to-hit and leave-to-goal straight segments.

stem: Two openings each subtend 20° at a point sensor. Their two limiting edge points are symmetrically placed at equal range R from the sensor: R=2 m for one opening and R=4 m for the other. Model the transverse opening width as the straight chord between its edge points. A circular robot has diameter 0.6 m and needs a 0.1 m margin on each side. Which widths and clearance conclusion follow?

options.text: Widths about 0.347 m and 0.695 m; neither opening meets the required clearance.
Widths about 1.368 m and 2.736 m; both openings meet the required clearance.
Widths about 0.695 m and 1.389 m; both openings meet the required clearance.
Widths about 0.695 m and 1.389 m; only the farther opening meets the required clearance.

assumptions: The symmetric chord model and all numbers are supplied, not inferred from the slide’s histogram.
The opening plane is perpendicular to its angular bisector, the traversed region is otherwise clear, and only the stated transverse clearance is tested.
Use exact trigonometric values for the comparison, then round reported widths to three decimals. Angular width alone does not establish full trajectory feasibility.

stem: A supplied VFH-style exercise has sector centers [0,30,60,90,120,150,180,210,240,270,300,330] degrees and corresponding densities [1,1,5,1,2,1,2,7,6,5,2,1]. Mark density >=5 blocked, and also block the 90° sector with a feasibility mask. A valley is a maximal circular run of remaining free sectors; use only runs of at least three sectors. Generate one candidate at each eligible run’s angular midpoint, unwrapping across 360° when needed. For each candidate θ, minimize G=5Δ(θ,20°)+2Δ(θ,150°)+2Δ(θ,150°), where Δ is the smaller absolute circular difference. The references are respectively goal, current heading and previous command. Which valleys and selected heading/cost result?

options.text: Valleys {300,330,0,30} and {120,150,180}; select 345° with cost 175.
Valleys {300,330,0,30} and {120,150,180}; select 150° with cost 650.

assumptions: The density vector, mask, equality convention, three-sector minimum and midpoint-only candidate policy are supplied deterministic exercise rules, not a claim to reproduce every VFH/VFH+ implementation detail.
Adjacent sectors include 330° and 0°. All values use the same fixed angular reference frame; the current heading and previous command both equal 150°.
The supplied mask and minimum run length are treated as the complete feasibility test for this toy decision. No unprinted certainty-grid weighting formula is inferred.
Choose the smallest numeric normalized heading if complete costs tie; no tie occurs here. The final selection is local, not a global route or real-robot safety guarantee.

stem: A gradient-following arm stalls at a differentiable, collision-free local minimum of its potential U, away from the goal. What is the central failure?

options.text: The local descent rule has no downhill direction there, even though a valid route may exist elsewhere.
Every local minimum must have zero potential value, so changing the potential’s constant offset removes the stall.
The arm has proved that no collision-free route exists in the complete configuration space.
Taking a smaller positive step along the same negative-gradient direction necessarily restarts motion.

assumptions: The controller uses only the negative potential gradient, with a positive scalar step factor and no noise, escape strategy or higher-level replanning.
